passage: The school trip bus was crawling through traffic, and Ma'am sat right at the front with her headphones in, listening for the guide's calls. At the back, Kunal grabbed Bittu's cap and tossed it around. "Catch it, baby!" Bittu's face crumpled under his fringe. Shreya, two rows ahead, felt her chest go tight. She wanted to say stop. But last month Kunal had poured water in Rupal's bag just for saying "leave it." Nazia, beside Shreya, laughed loudly, then whispered, "I'm only laughing so he won't start on us." Two boys joined in the throwing. Everyone else looked out of the window. Shreya looked at the front. Surely someone would tell Ma'am. Nobody did. The bus crawled on, and so did the game.

qa.q: What did Kunal grab from Bittu?
qa.a: He grabbed Bittu's cap and tossed it around.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling as she watched?
qa.a: She felt sorry for Bittu and wanted to say stop, but she was afraid Kunal would target her the way he had targeted Rupal.

qa.q: What small step could one of the bystanders take right now?
qa.a: Shreya could walk up and quietly tell Ma'am, or several children could together say "give it back," instead of each waiting for someone else.

qa.q: How does the bus look from Bittu's seat?
qa.a: To Bittu it probably looks like everyone is either laughing or ignoring him, so he feels completely alone, even though many feel sorry for him.

grounding: It shows classmates who pity the target but fear being next, some laughing to stay safe or joining in, all waiting for someone else to act.

passage: At the building-block club in the society clubhouse in Pune, Mridul kept pushing Gaurav's tower over. "Oops. Clumsy Gaurav," he said, and a few kids laughed. Eshaan sat at the next table, clicking two blocks together and apart, together and apart. He liked Gaurav. They had walked home together once. But Mridul was bigger, and Eshaan didn't want to be the next tower on the floor. When Mridul said, "Right, Eshaan?" Eshaan gave a small laugh and hated himself for it. Across the room, Aisha frowned but kept building. Eshaan thought, Aisha will say something, she's brave. Aisha was probably thinking the same about him. Gaurav picked up his blocks slowly, one by one, not looking at anyone.

qa.q: What did Mridul keep pushing over?
qa.a: He kept pushing Gaurav's tower over.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan hate himself after laughing?
qa.a: He liked Gaurav and knew the laugh was wrong, but fear of Mridul made him go along.

qa.q: What would you advise Eshaan to try next time?
qa.a: He could sit with Gaurav and help rebuild, or tell the club supervisor afterwards, without needing to fight Mridul.

qa.q: What would change if Eshaan and Aisha spoke up together?
qa.a: Mridul would lose his laughing audience, and Gaurav would see that he is not alone.

grounding: It illustrates kind children who pity the target but laugh or stay quiet from fear, each waiting for another to act.

passage:
"Hafsa, did you see what they did to Rohit's lunch today?"

"I saw, Bhavna. They put sand in it."

"And everyone laughed."

"You laughed too."

"Only a little! If I didn't laugh, they'd look at me next."

"I didn't laugh. But I didn't do anything either."

"Nobody did. Megha even threw a bit of sand."

"Megha's nice, though."

"I know. She was probably scared too."

"Somebody should tell Ma'am."

"Somebody. Not me. They'd call me a tattletale."

"That's what everyone thinks. So nobody tells."

"...So what do we do?"

"Maybe we tell Ma'am together. Then it's not just one of us."

"Ma'am, can we tell you something about Rohit?"

"Of course. Thank you both for coming. I'll speak to those boys right now.""

qa.q: What did the boys put in Rohit's lunch?
qa.a: Sand.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna laugh even though she felt bad?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she didn't laugh, the bullies would look at her next.

qa.q: What does Hafsa suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Telling Ma'am together, so no one child has to be alone or feel like a tattletale.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel when even nice classmates laugh?
qa.a: He probably feels humiliated and alone, thinking nobody is on his side.

grounding: Hafsa and Bhavna, as bystanders, feel sorry but fear being next, admit laughing or staying silent, and each waits for someone else to act.

passage:
I remember the week Suraj stopped coming to the playground. I was one of the kids who watched.

It started with the older boys calling him "Moti" and pulling his shirt. Most of us felt bad. I felt bad. But when they looked around, I laughed along with everyone. It felt safer. If I didn't laugh, maybe they'd start on me.

Then Pinku, who was always kind, actually joined in and pushed Suraj. I couldn't believe it. Later Pinku told me, "If I'm with them, they won't pick me."

We all kept thinking somebody else would tell the teacher. Somebody braver. Nobody did, for weeks.

There were twenty of us, most of us nice, and it still happened in front of all of us. In the end Suraj's grandmother saw his torn shirt and went straight to the principal.

— Deepika

qa.q: What nickname did the older boys call Suraj?
qa.a: "Moti".

qa.q: How does Deepika feel, looking back on laughing along?
qa.a: Deepika feels guilty and regretful, having laughed out of fear of becoming the next target.

qa.q: What could one child in that class have done?
qa.a: Tell a teacher, or ask a few friends to tell together, instead of waiting for someone braver.

qa.q: What was it like for Suraj to see twenty classmates watch and do nothing?
qa.a: He probably felt completely alone and ashamed, which is why he stopped coming to the playground.

grounding: Deepika recalls being a bystander who laughed out of fear while kind classmates watched or joined, each waiting for someone else to act.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5, Wednesday

At recess I watched the children around Ravi, who is teased about his limp.

Two boys mimicked his walk while about ten children watched. Chandrika, one of my kindest students, looked upset and stepped back, but did not leave. Three others laughed, glancing at the boys as they did, as if checking it was the right thing. One girl joined in the mimicking briefly and then stopped.

Nobody came to tell me. Each seemed to be waiting for someone else.

After recess I spoke to the two boys. In the last period I talked to the whole class about what they can do when they see unkindness: stand with the child, and tell an adult. I also spoke to Ravi and his mother after school.

— Nirmala Ma'am

qa.q: What did the two boys do to Ravi?
qa.a: They mimicked his walk.

qa.q: How did Chandrika seem to feel during recess?
qa.a: Chandrika seemed upset and uneasy, stepping back but not leaving or speaking.

qa.q: How did Nirmala Ma'am respond after recess, and why does it help?
qa.a: She spoke to the two boys, taught the class how to stand with a child and tell an adult, and talked to Ravi and his mother after school.

qa.q: Why might the three children laugh while glancing at the boys?
qa.a: They may have felt afraid of becoming targets and laughed to stay safe, checking the boys approved.

grounding: A teacher's note shows kind children watching, laughing or joining in out of fear while each waits for someone else to act, and the teacher's response.

passage:
Tuesday
At recess Deepak's gang took Kalyani's tiffin again and passed it around over her head. Kalyani didn't cry. She just stood there with empty hands. I felt sick. Ruchi laughed, but I think she only laughed so they wouldn't pick her next. Imran even threw it once. The rest of us just watched. I kept waiting for someone else to do something, Pooja who is brave, or the monitor, but everyone was waiting too. Twenty kind kids, doing nothing.
At dinner I told Ammi. She put down her spoon and listened to all of it. She said I was right to tell her, and she wrote to Kalyani's class teacher before I went to bed.
I'm still ashamed I did nothing at recess.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Deepak's gang do with Kalyani's tiffin?
qa.a: They took it and passed it around over her head.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling while watching at recess?
qa.a: Sabina felt sick and ashamed, wanting someone to act but frozen, waiting like everyone else.

qa.q: What could one child in that crowd have done?
qa.a: One child could have stood beside Kalyani and said 'give it back', or gone straight to a teacher, instead of waiting for someone braver.

qa.q: What is it like for Kalyani when the whole crowd just watches?
qa.a: Kalyani probably feels alone and humiliated, standing with empty hands while nobody helps.

grounding: Shows classmates who feel sorry for a bullied girl yet laugh, join in or wait for someone else, so a group of kind children still allows harm.
